questions.q: What is the default Pod-to-Pod networking behavior in a Kubernetes cluster with no NetworkPolicy resources?
options: Only Pods in the same namespace can reach each other
All Pod-to-Pod traffic is blocked until explicitly allowed
Traffic is allowed only between Pods with identical labels
Every Pod can reach every other Pod, regardless of namespace — there is no network segmentation by default
questions.explain: Kubernetes networking is open by default — isolation is opt-in via NetworkPolicy, not opt-out. Without any policies, nothing restricts Pod-to-Pod traffic.

questions.q: Northbridge writes a correct NetworkPolicy but traffic still isn't being restricted. What is the most likely cause?
options: The cluster's CNI plugin doesn't implement NetworkPolicy enforcement, so the rules are silently ignored
NetworkPolicy only works with NodePort Services
NetworkPolicy objects require a paid Kubernetes license
NetworkPolicy objects must be created before any Pods exist
questions.explain: NetworkPolicy enforcement depends on the CNI plugin supporting it (e.g. Calico, Cilium, Antrea). Some simpler CNI plugins accept the objects but don't actually enforce them.

questions.q: In a NetworkPolicy, what does a podSelector: {} with policyTypes [Ingress, Egress] and no ingress/egress rules listed accomplish?
options: It allows all traffic for every Pod in the namespace
It applies only to Pods explicitly labeled 'deny'
It matches every Pod in the namespace and blocks all inbound and outbound traffic for them — a default-deny-all
It has no effect since no rules are specified
questions.explain: An empty podSelector matches all Pods in the namespace. With policyTypes set but no corresponding rules, no traffic is permitted — this is the standard default-deny pattern.

questions.q: In the allow-checkout-to-payments policy, what does the top-level podSelector (matchLabels app: payment-processing) determine, versus the podSelector nested inside the 'from' block?
options: The top-level podSelector picks which Pods the policy applies TO; the nested one under 'from' picks which Pods are allowed to send traffic IN
The top-level selector controls egress only; the nested one controls ingress only
The nested podSelector overrides the top-level one
They do the same thing and one is redundant
questions.explain: The policy's own podSelector scopes which Pods it governs (payment-processing). The podSelector inside an ingress rule's 'from' list specifies which source Pods are permitted to reach them (checkout).

questions.q: If two NetworkPolicy objects both select the same Pod — one default-deny and one narrow allow rule — how do they combine?
options: The policies are additive; the Pod's effective rules are the union of every policy that selects it
Only the default-deny policy takes effect; allow rules are ignored
The policies conflict and Kubernetes rejects the second one
Only the most recently created policy applies
questions.explain: NetworkPolicies are additive — when multiple policies select the same Pod, the effective allowed traffic is the union of all their rules, which is why default-deny-then-allow works as a layered pattern.
